speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word concerning the representations made last week by a delegation from Elliot Lake, and the course the government intends to take in regard thereto.
The government is most desirous of continuing to work with the government of Ontario to find a solution to the problem. The Minister of Labour has advised the government of Ontario that the federal government desires to co-operate and participate in the cost of any useful training program for those of the miners who will be laid off in consequence of the decision of the United States not to undertake to take any more uranium than is provided for in the agreements which were entered into several years ago.
As the house knows, Elliot Lake was last week declared a labour surplus area, and the efforts of the national employment service to find alternative job openings have intensified. Furthermore, a fact-finding group will immediately be sent by the government to Elliot Lake, consisting of representatives of the national employment service, the unemployment insurance commission and the industrial development branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. These officials will assemble information on the range and variety of labour supply, the resources of the area and alternative development possibilities. They will consider the problem of alternative employment, the retraining of workers, industrial development prospects, and will consult with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation concerning the problems of home owners.
On their return to Ottawa they will report their findings. The group which will be leaving this evening for the area in question consists of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour; Mr. A. F. Mac Arthur, commissioner of the unemployment insurance commission; Mr. W. M. Hall and Mr. G. A. Cooper, industrial development branch, Department of Trade and Commerce. After the report has been considered the Minister of 79951-0-113
Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour will then visit Elliot Lake, but that will not take place before the expiration of a week or so.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: I am sure all the inhabitants of the area in question will welcome this evidence of concern on the part of the government over the difficulties that are facing them. I am sure they would have welcomed even more a visit by the Prime Minister, especially after the very warm welcome he gave their delegation last week. We can only hope that this visit, followed as it will be by a visit of the ministers, will result in positive action which will help this community out of the difficulties it is now facing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: If I may be allowed, because of the personal reference to myself, I should like to say this. Naturally these women representatives of Elliot Lake were received in a spirit of deep regard and sympathy. They presented their case reasonably and fairly. They asked me whether I would myself visit the area. I pointed out to them the fact that my immediate reaction was that were I to do so it might have the result of raising unjustified hopes on the part of the residents and workers. Having reconsidered my remarks at that time I am reinforced in that viewpoint, and feel that the most effective action would be along the line indicated by me a moment ago.

subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
We in this party welcome the statement by the Prime Minister as to an investigation and report that is to be made. We in this party tried to make it clear that investigation and study should have been made before this thing ever happened. According to the statement by the Prime Minister they are now sending in an investigation committee.
I do not know how many times we have asked this government to consider what was going to happen before it took place. I refer particularly to Elliot Lake because it was known at the time-not under the Prime Minister's aegis but under that of the Liberal government-that only a certain period was set forth under direct contract. What has happened since then? Because of the mistake- and I use that word advisedly-of the previous government a town has been built up, one of the most magnificent in the record of our country, because of a certain requirement.

Proposed Legislation
I am not blaming the Prime Minister for what has happened. As a matter of fact I am going to say that more than anybody else I am blaming the previous government for what has happened.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is departing a bit from the customary type of comment at this stage. This is not a debate. He is free to comment on the statement that has been made.

subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE, ONT.  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
That is what I am trying to do, Mr. Speaker, namely, to comment on the statement by the Prime Minister as to what the present government is planning to do now because of the situation at Elliot Lake. I am convinced that this procedure is in order. We have there the finest example as to the meaning of planning which only this party has asked this government to do; I refer to real planning.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether, in view of what is now being done in planning five or seven years too late, he will consider and have passed by his government legislation giving recognition to the need for planning all across Canada in what is developing under his system of private enterprise? Will he look into that matter now?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is getting rather far into the realm of fancy, and his question is hypothetical concerning government practice in general.

I have a question to ask on the Bomarc sites. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think we are losing all sense of proportion in this matter. I might say that so far as the Bomarc A was concerned, which was the previous type of missile, there were 80 tests made before it became operational. There have been seven tests made of this Bomarc B. While there have been some failures in the component parts of the apparatus, those who are responsible for the development believe these can be overcome.
Inquiries of the Ministry
I might mention that the United States, in this fiscal year, is spending $421.5 million for the development of Bomarc sites across this continent, of which there are 18 interlocking sites. Two of these will be constructed in Canada. The United States is providing an amount of over $70 million for the provision of the missiles and launching equipment for these two sites. Canada is contributing $15 million, of which somewhere around $300,000 has already been spent on preliminary work and the acquisition of land.
Now, I have had assurances as recently as this morning, when I was talking on the telephone to the secretary for defence of the United States, that if there is any change to be made at all in the defence program for the North American continent under NORAD, Canada will be consulted before any decisions are made.

Before I ask my question I should like to take this opportunity to thank members on both sides of the house and members of the press gallery who, while I was in hospital, cheered me up with their cards and notes.
I should now like to direct a question to the Prime Minister supplementary to that asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West. My question is based on a report that appeared in the Sudbury Star of January 27 with respect to an interview with Mr. Gillis who dealt with a conference he had had with the Prime Minister with regard to pension vesting. The report states in part:
The Prime Minister told Gillis he would inquire as to why the clause had been deleted and would talk over with national revenue minister Nowlan and other members of the cabinet the advisability of reinstating it.
I wonder whether the Prime Minister could explain to the house how this order in council was passed without the knowledge of the head of the government? Second, can he tell the house why this clause was deleted from the Income Tax Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING PENSION VESTING PROVISIONS OF ACT
speechtext:
There was no order in council to that effect that I know anything about. I think the hon. member is misinformed. The situation was simply this; that in June, 1950, the former minister of national revenue, Hon. Dr. McCann, caused to be published a blue book respecting pension plans for purposes of the Income Tax Act. Paragraph 10B of this book contains a statement respecting vesting to which attention is called by Mr. Gillis.
[Mr. Herridge.)

Now, I do not want to go into the history of this. This was simply a statement in a booklet issued by the minister and under the authority of the department which, according to my information, was not regarded by the department as in any way binding. In 1959 it was deleted, and Mr. Gillis raised with me the question as to reinstituting this particular section, not because of its legal authority but simply because, having been in the former blue book, it should be continued.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING PENSION VESTING PROVISIONS OF ACT
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. Is it not correct that this clause was deleted as the result of an order in council or other order published in the Canada Gazette on July 18 of last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING PENSION VESTING PROVISIONS OF ACT
speechtext: I have pointed out the facts as they are given to me respecting this particular section. I pointed out that there was no order in council that rendered ineffective the efficacy of section 10B, and that whatever the effect of 10B may have been there was no deletion of the legal effect under an order in council.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING PENSION VESTING PROVISIONS OF ACT
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister another supplementary question. In view of the Prime Minister's answer, why would he listen to appeals from Mr. Gillis and the officers of this union for the restoration of this right, which in their brief to the government they said had been affected by an order published on July 18 of last year?

placed before me their representations, which I viewed as being based upon a reasonable request, and I stated that consideration would have to be given by the various departments affected. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the object of an amendment to the motion to go into supply is twofold. In the first place it is to express a point of view different from that which is contained in the motion. Next, it is because the public has a grievance which the opposition desires to bring to the attention of the house and of the country.
In the present case the opposition says that the government by its policies has done three things which are not in the public interest. First, it is giving away Canadian sovereignty in the air. Next, it is discriminating against small air lines in favour of the larger and more powerful ones, and in turn discriminating against the outlying areas of the country. Third, the opposition say the government cannot seem to make up its mind on the kind of air terminals that it wants to build in this country.
Even if everything done by the former administration was wrong-and that is something which I am not prepared to admit- surely after the government has been in office for a period of three years, it should know by this time what it wants. It should know what to do. It should be able to stand on its own feet. It ought to be able to put right all those things which it said were wrong heretofore.
Instead of that the government is going in all directions in the three fields I have mentioned, namely in the field of international air service, the field of domestic air service and the field of the construction of terminals. It has no clear goal before it. There is confusion and uncertainty in these three fields

of civil aviation. Since this government has been in office I ask where there has been a clear-cut declaration of government policy in these fields. Where has there been an over-all attempt to deal with these matters?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he will find it more comfortable if he has a little more attention from the house. There seems to be an undue amount of conversation today, and I am afraid it is interrupting the speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RESPECT TO CIVIL AVIATION
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was saying, where has there been an overall attempt to deal with these matters in a statement of government policy? Instead we have ad hoc decisions. We have decisions that deal with cases which come up from time to time, and it is impossible either for the public or the air industry to know what the position of the government is.
Since this government has been in office it has placed in jeopardy the once favourable position held by Canada in the field of international aviation. Prior to 1957 Canada had a well defined policy in the negotiation of bilateral air agreements. It held generally to the position of exchanging third and fourth freedoms only with other countries, because to go beyond that would be against the national interest.
Since this government has been in office several concessions have been granted to European countries, and a number of additional services have been permitted to come into being between Canada and Europe which have been detrimental to our own country. In some cases the concessions have involved fifth freedom rights to the air carriers of other countries without Canada receiving reciprocal rights or reciprocal privileges in return. Specifically, the rights which have been given away are as follows:
1.	The granting of fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago to the air carriers of France and West Germany.
2.	The naming of Toronto as an additional point of call for the British air carrier.
3.	The granting of additional rights to the air carriers of the United States, and;
4.	The granting of fifth freedom rights to an Italian carrier between Montreal and Mexico, Montreal and Chicago and Montreal and Los Angeles.
In short, the international air negotiations which have taken place during the last two years have branded Canada as an easy mark, and as a result other European nations are indicating that they would like to reopen air discussions with our country, obviously looking to the improvement of their position and the deterioration of ours.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
I would like now, sir, to put on the record and examine each of the bilateral air agreements or the amendments thereto negotiated since this government has been in office, and I would like to consider what the position is today and what damage has been done to our own country in the field of international air navigation.
First I would deal with France. For some time prior to 1957 the Liberal administration had been under constant pressure from the French government for a revision of the existing air agreement between Canada and France so as to provide for the carriage of local traffic-that is fifth freedom traffic

by the French carrier between Montreal and Chicago in both directions, with France being willing to concede, on the other hand, the granting of rights to a Canadian carrier for the carriage of local traffic between Paris and a point in Europe to be designated by Canada, Rome or Vienna being specifically mentioned.
The pressure which was exercised against the former administration was resisted because of two reasons; first, because the former administration did not think there was a sufficient quid pro quo in what was being offered by the government of France; and next, because no Canadian carrier possessed non-stop rights between Montreal and Chicago and it was thought at the time that if the government was not successful in itself obtaining from the United States non-stop rights between Montreal and Chicago, it should not concede those onward rights to another country.
It should be mentioned at this stage that Canada has a route under its bilateral agreement with the United States which provides for a flight to Chicago, but on condition that that flight come down at Toronto, and in consequence any Canadian flights which originate at Montreal for Chicago must make a Toronto stop.
Following the two elections of 1957 and 1958, the present government yielded to the pressure of the French government and granted fifth freedom rights to the French carrier between Montreal and Chicago, which became effective in November, 1958. In return Canada has received from the French government fifth freedom rights between Paris and Rome or Vienna, which rights have not been implemented by Canada because of failure to obtain similar rights from other countries concerned. It should also be emphasized here that during this period the Canadian government has been entirely unsuccessful in obtaining rights from the United States for a Montreal-Chicago route.
Thus, sir, Air France has been able to enjoy traffic rights between Montreal and
Civil Aviation
Chicago without direct competition from a Canadian carrier, and this is truly a sad commentary on the ability of a Canadian delegation to negotiate bilateral air agreements or amendments thereto. Furthermore, this amendment to the bilateral agreement with the country now under discussion has had a considerable and serious detrimental effect upon the revenues of Canadian carriers.
I should like next to deal with the air agreement with West Germany. In 1958 a meeting was held between representatives of Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany having for its object the negotiation of a formal bilateral air agreement to supersede the temporary arrangement for air services between the two countries then in effect. The negotiations culminated in an agreement being reached on a mutually equitable basis for air service between the two countries, but in addition granting to Germany fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago in return for Canadian fifth freedom rights between Dusseldorf and Vienna. It was also agreed that future fifth freedom rights would be granted to Germany between Montreal and Boston or New York, coincidental with the granting to Canada of fifth freedom rights between Dusseldorf and a point in Europe to be determined by Canada.
This, sir, was a reasonable agreement with the exception of the exchange of Montreal-Chicago for Dusseldorf-Vienna, where the balance is highly in favour of the German carrier because of the difference in the volume of traffic over the two routes. There is no comparison between the onward rights from Montreal to Chicago and those from Dusseldorf to Vienna. It is again emphasized here that Canada granted privileges to a foreign carrier to operate over a route not already granted to its own air carrier and for which it has not since been successful in obtaining such rights. Again in this instance there has been a considerable loss of revenue to Canada as in the agreement with the French government.
I come now to the bilateral agreement, or its revision, with the United States. The bilateral air agreement signed between Canada and the United States dates back, I believe, to 1949. It was amended in 1955 and further amended in April of 1959. Under that agreement provision was made for the addition of a number of short haul trans-border routes highly favourable to the United States and equally unfavourable to Canada, thus placing in imbalance what had theretofore been mutually acceptable treatment. None of the hopes and desires of the Canadian companies were given serious consideration, and the entire negotiations were

speechtext:
In order to save the time of the house I shall not give consideration to those rights which are given to the United States as opposed to Canada. I shall simply make this comment, though; that if one examines this table it will readily be seen that the list of additions does little or nothing to further the cause of Canadian aviation, but that it does a great deal to further the cause of United States aviation, providing as it does for a number of additional gateway points from which traffic can be distributed to larger centres of population, and hampering the development of direct services between Canada and these larger centres. In addition to this, the new routes fit in much better with the United States pattern than with the Canadian pattern.
To bring the matter into proper focus, every pressure must now be brought to bear to induce the United States to agree to a complete renegotiation of the air agreement so as to open up additional centres of dense population for direct air services from Canada. It should be noted in passing that the United States has been far more generous to its European friends than it has been to Canada. The United States seems to have had no difficulty whatsoever about granting onward rights in its own country to European

carriers such as Alitalia, Sabena, Air France, Lufthansa and the like, although not granting those onward rights to Canadian carriers.
I submit that this situation must be corrected, but that can only be done if there is a more realistic and forceful approach to the problem by the present government. Lack of correction can only mean the sale of Canada's birthright for the proverbial mess of pottage, at least as far as aviation is concerned. We do not, in this country, go to the bargaining table with empty hands. On the contrary, it has been stated repeatedly, and it is a fact, that no air line that wants to travel the world routes can do so without crossing Canadian territory at some point or other. Moreover, a goodly portion of air travel between Canada and the United States originates in Canadian centres and our people, I submit, deserve the right to be carried to their destinations in aircraft owned and operated by Canadian air lines rather than be transferred to United States carriers at the first gateway point within that country, with all the inconvenience and difficulty which that is likely to bring about. Obviously Canada must bring pressure to bear. The United States is, of course, quite satisfied and complacent about the whole

situation as it exists today. That is natural, because the position is one which is satisfactory to the United States.
I turn now to the agreement with the United Kingdom. At the invitation of the British government, talks relating to a revision of the bilateral air agreement were held in Ottawa in May, 1959, and culminated in the British being granted the use of Toronto as a terminal airport in Canada in addition to Montreal. This gives the United Kingdom direct access to both of Canada's largest traffic generating centres. There was no gift within the power of the British to compensate for this tremendous right which Canada gave up, and as a result Canada came out second best at the negotiating table with the United Kingdom; because that concession is having, as it was bound to have, a serious effect on the revenue position of Canadian carriers. That is a sad situation, because there is no doubt in my mind that this is what has brought about the pooling of resources between one of the Canadian carriers and its British counterpart. A sad situation, this, and one which I am sure would not have become worthy of consideration a few short years ago.
What price did the British pay for obtaining this prize concession allowing them to enter the Toronto market, which is by far the most lucrative air market in this country? They agreed to the inclusion of the additional point, Toronto, on the existing Vancouver-Hong Kong route, and the granting of fifth freedom privileges between the United Kingdom and certain European points, all of doubtful value at the time they were given and of even less value today with the advent of the jet era and large aircraft requiring long-range flights before they are economic in operation. What good, for instance, is the London-Brussels fifth freedom concession in these circumstances, more particularly when Canada would be required to grant a further concession to the Belgians in order to implement it? This was but another case of Canada failing to meet fire with fire and being outmanoeuvered at the bargaining table because of lack of tenacity of purpose and, apparently, an inherent fear of failure to reach agreement. Sir, it is better that there should be no agreement, than one without honour or equity.
Last, but not least, is this air agreement with Italy, which it seems to me cannot be explained by any stretch of the imagination. If ever a country gave away rights Canada did in the case of its bilateral air agreement with Italy. The recent negotiation of the agreement between Canada and Italy offers, I say, a prize example of a give-away program
Civil Aviation
so far as this country is concerned, and one which has justly earned Canada the name of being an easy mark as far as international bargaining is concerned.
The primary function of any bilateral air agreement is to provide for air services between the two countries involved. In this case the main object appears to have been completely lost sight of if one judges by the many and various other rights and privileges which have been written into the agreement. An outline of this and a comment thereon would appear to be in order at the present time.
Canada did, of course, obtain third and fourth freedom rights between Montreal and Rome. In addition it obtained fifth freedom rights between Lisbon and Rome and between Rome and Bangkok, as well as the possibility of Paris to Rome. Italy, on the other hand, obtained third and fourth freedom rights between Rome and Montreal, and in addition it was granted fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago, Montreal and Los Angeles and Montreal and Mexico.
Let us look at the comparison between these exchanges. On the one hand we have Lisbon-Rome versus Montreal-Chicago. What comparison is there? Montreal-Chicago is a lucrative route and unquestionably highly desired by any air carrier. Montreal-Lisbon is not nearly as attractive, I would say. The comparison here, sir, is that of a horse for a rabbit or, perhaps better, an elephant for a mouse, which latter term might well be descriptive of the timidity of Canada at the bargaining table.
Then we come to a comparison of Rome-Bangkok versus Montreal-Los Angeles and here words literally fail me, because there is nothing in my vocabulary which can actually describe the situation. There may be a lot of people who want to travel Montreal to Los Angeles, but who wants to travel Montreal to Bangkok? Who on earth by way of a fifth freedom privilege wants to go to Bangkok? There may be some people, but the exchange of those two routes is, I say, simply ridiculous.
Adding to the state of imbalance, what did Canada do? It did not think that was enough. It threw in, over and above the bargain, Montreal-Mexico City versus Paris-Rome out of pure sympathy for the Italian position. Surely it can be said with effective and absolute conviction that never has so much been given for so little to the obvious detriment of Canadian industry.
I ask what are the effects on Canada of these new bilaterals, additional amendments and revisions to older bilaterals, because of government action? What sense of urgency, I ask, has caused the government of Canada to

Civil Aviation
enter into such one-sided arrangements as those which have been negotiated recently? Why have not the exorbitant demands of other countries been rejected? What does the government intend to do now in order to restore the reputation of Canada so far as its ability to conduct fair and equitable air negotiations is concerned? By virtue of its own actions Canada has become the laughingstock of the world with respect to air negotiations. This deplorable situation must not be allowed to continue.
The first obvious step for correction is an abandonment of this ad hoc policy pursued by the government with respect to international aviation since its inception and the development and implementation of a long term program based on sound reasoning, economic feasibility and development of this country's air transportation industry rather than the granting of rights indiscriminately to air carriers of other countries.
The cumulative effect of this give-away program of the past two years has been the loss of millions of dollars in gross and net revenues to Canadian air carriers, with a consequent reduction in their rate of expansion and a consequent reduction in employment to Canadians. I state here that because of these arrangements the air industry has become apprehensive of the loss of employment, as I intend to show later on.
Then there is also the fact that every inequitable concession which has been granted to foreign air carriers brings with it a reduction in potential so far as revenue is concerned, not only in the air lines themselves but also in the related services, in the supply industries and in those industries which are responsible for keeping the civil aviation industry on its feet, to say the least. In the natural course of events Canada suffers to some degree also in the field of international aviation in comparison with European countries because of the higher wage rates that obtain in this country. Let us not add to our own problems by granting undue concession to these carriers to further weaken our position.
There is also the establishment in Europe of the air union. The air union, as the house knows, is a sort of common market in the air made up of four carriers including Alitalia Air France, Lufthansa and Sabena, the object of which is to travel the north Atlantic run and other runs in co-ordination with each other and unquestionably at the expense of our own carriers. Picture for a moment the result of the co-ordination of scheduling by the three carriers, Air France, Lufthansa and Alitalia, which have already possession of onward rights from Montreal

to Chicago. Picture again what complete co-ordination on the north Atlantic can do to Canada. It is the responsibility of the government to be alert to these situations and ensure that nothing is done by the air union carriers, either individually or collectively, which is incompatible with the letter and intent of the various bilateral air agreements which Canada has entered into from time to time with the countries concerned.
Vigilance must be exercised continually to ensure that the interests of our own carriers are protected to the utmost degree, and that their rights and privileges are not abrogated. The conclusion which follows in this field, from what I have said and from the series of events I have outlined which have taken place during the last two years, or will undoubtedly occur as a result of things to come, is serious, particularly as it would affect the revenue field. To place an accurate dollar value on such items is a difficult task, and I am not going to attempt to say what it means by way of loss of revenue; but I would put it in the realm of $5 million in gross revenues in 1959 for the Canadian carriers and in the realm of $7,500,000 in gross revenues in 1960, with that amount becoming progressively greater in the years to come.
All of this leads to the conclusion that what the government has done is a serious matter. I am confirmed in that conclusion by an order in council which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) tabled in the house the other day, P.C. 1960/92, which was filed under section 80 of the Financial Administration Act covering the capital budget of Trans-Canada Air Lines for the year 1960. Here the minister tells us that T.C.A. will require for 1960 the sum of $97,500,000 made up of approximately $83 million for property and equipment, $4 million for refinancing of loans and $10 million for increased material and supplies. There follows this significant statement: "Source of funds: Net income, nil."
Therefore, while this is not a conclusive deduction, nevertheless it appears from this statement filed by the minister that T.C.A. will not have a net income for the year 1959 compared with previous years when it always did. We will not know this definitely, of course, until the minister tables the annual report of Trans-Canada Air Lines but if it follows what is indicated in this budget it will show a deficit for the year 1959. My contention is that if there is a deficit it is due to the policy of the government in opening up to competition in the international field air routes and air privileges to which this country normally would be entitled.
This is the third time that I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter, once

outside the house and the second time in the house. The minister has not seen fit to reply on any occasion. On a previous occasion when I discussed the matter in the house he dismissed it by the comment "nonsense" to a reporter who spoke to him outside the house. I am not offended by the fact that he would dismiss this rather serious allegation on the part of the opposition as nonsense but I think that allegations of such a serious character are at least deserving of a reply from the minister other than the word "nonsense".
But the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), in an attempt to right what had been said, asked the minister on the orders of the day how many more Canadians would be able to travel by air directly from Canada this year than would have been able to do so under the bilateral agreements in operation previously. The minister, with great satisfaction, rose and replied that under the agreements negotiated by the present government it was estimated that 40,000 more Canadians would be able to travel directly from Canada to other countries than would have been able to do so under the arrangements worked out by the late lamented Liberal government. I say, sir, that that is not an answer to the charges which we are making.
I say it is not an answer because, first of all, I ask how this figure of 40,000 is arrived at and, second, if it should be accurate then I point out that it could have been obtained just as easily through the negotiations with the French government because under the former bilateral negotiated by the Liberal administration Canada already had the right to obtain fifth freedom rights from Paris to Rome. Therefore the Canadian government was under no obligation to negotiate another air agreement with Italy. It could have completed the negotiations with the French government and obtained for the Canadian carrier the same rights as were obtained in the Italian agreement for another Canadian carrier. Therefore if the point made by the hon. member for Vancouver South holds, it certainly holds also in connection with the other agreement with the French government whereby it would not have been necessary to grant all these additional rights to the government of Italy. But I add this.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will answer in a moment.
What difference does it make if a new air agreement makes it possible for 100,000 more Canadians to travel rather than 40,000 or 10,000 if because of that additional travel there is going to be a loss of revenue in the budgets and the profit and loss statements of the various Canadian carriers? That is a figure
Civil Aviation
that I have already put on Hansard, namely a loss of some $5 million to $7.5 million in gross revenues.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

With reference to landing rights at Bangkok, which seemed to lead to a great deal of merriment, is it quite fair for the hon. member not to indicate that this is but one step to enable around the world flights by Canadian Pacific Air Lines? That is not the end of it. It is a filling-in step.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My friend is quite right but here is the point. In going around the world you have to negotiate with other governments. The moment you go on to Bangkok you have to negotiate with the government of that country and you have to negotiate with other governments. When you negotiate with other governments you have to give up rights in your own country. That is what I am trying to establish and I believe I have succeeded in establishing that we have given far too much to other governments in exchange for the rights we have received.

Would the hon. member permit another question? How long did it take the former administration to get landing rights in New York for T.C.A. on the Montreal-New York run? Eastern Air Lines had a monopoly of that traffic and held on to it by embargos, injunctions and so on. How long did it take you to do something there?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My friend is now following the tactics of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) by asking a question and succeeding in making a speech. I dealt with the air agreement with the United States and I said that it was the practice of the former administration to exchange third and fourth freedom rights for similar rights in other countries. There are some exceptions to that but not very many. But in the amendments to the United States agreement made by the present government the government went much further than we did and it made a bad bargain in so far as Canada is concerned as will be seen if you will look at the chart which I have already put on Hansard.
I say that this is not the way, by answering questions on the orders of the day by press releases from the minister's office, to deal with matters of this importance. I repeat that if it is only a question of ignoring the person who is now speaking it makes no

Civil Aviation
difference but where it does make a difference is that it is ignoring the representatives of the aviation industry. If the minister wants to ignore the air industries and transport association, who at their annual meeting and in a brief presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) complained very bitterly about the minister and the attitude of the government, that is another thing. It is a far more serious matter which the minister must, of course, take cognizance of.
The difficulty about this whole matter, I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, is that the government has not placed on Hansard or anywhere else a clear-cut definition of its policy in the international air transportation field. We are entitled to know what that policy is. The government has been in office now for three years and they should tell the Canadian people what that policy is. I say that it has failed, completely and dismally, in so far as the field of international aviation is concerned.
I come now to the policy of the government in the field of domestic air services. This policy was announced by the minister, again in answer to a question by the same member, the hon. member for Vancouver South. On July 14, 1958, the Minister of Transport stated that the government, after studying this matter which was the regulation of non-scheduled services in the field of light aircraft, had come to the conclusion that there should be an easing in the terms of applications for licences for non-scheduled commercial air services which involve only the use of small, light aircraft and helicopters. He stated at page 2207 of Hansard of that date:
-the government has accordingly decided that it would be in the public interest that licences for air services using only this small type of aircraft be granted freely on request.
What, in effect, the government was doing by that statement was decontrolling what is known in the service as group C type aircraft. This policy caused untold harm in the air transport industry, and the air industries transport association, at its annual meeting in Montreal, protested vigorously. I hold in my hand a resolution which was passed on October 26, 1959. Since it is short, I should like to put it on Hansard. It reads:
Whereas a series of events have occurred over the past eighteen months which are cause for concern on the part of the air transport industry, chief among those being the actions of the Minister of Transport in declaring a wide-open licensing policy so far as class C operations are concerned, and a recent judgment reversing a decision of the air transport board relating to helicopter operations and extending such policy to large helicopters;
Whereas the air industries transport association of Canada endorses the principle that there should
[Mr. Chevrier.l
be competition within the air transport industry, where such competition is economically feasible;
And whereas it is the opinion of the association that each potential operator seeking a licence should be required-[DOT]
And I underline this.
-to prove both public interest and economic justification to the air transport board, and the weight of this evidence should be the governing factor in the granting or denying of a licence;
And whereas it is the opinion of the association that there is lacking a well defined Canadian air transportation policy, and that such policy is of vital necessity and in the public interest;
And therefore, be it resolved:
1.	That the federal government be urged to promulgate without undue delay, a sound and well defined air transport policy for Canada.
2.	That this policy should be of a long term nature and not be subject to fluctuation based on the exigencies of individual situations.
3.	That with the promulgation of such a policy full responsibility for its administration be placed in the hands of the air transport board.
The minister apparently paid no attention to this protest or this resolution which was approved at the annual convention of the air industries transport association because he further decontrolled the field, according to press release No. 1093, dated December 18, 1959. This action was designed to provide for the still more liberal granting of licences, a more extensive degree of competition in the field of non-scheduled commercial air services. The minister stated in this press release, and I quote:
A continuing review of this situation has led to the conclusion that the same policy should now be extended to apply to any non-scheduled charter service performed by helicopters and also to any non-scheduled charter service performed by mediumsized aircraft of the type defined by the air transport board as group B which, generally speaking, includes aircraft up to but not including the DC-3 size.
So the minister, according to this press release, went a step further and proceeded to decontrol the group B class type of aircraft. The air industries transport association, when they saw that their protest was of no avail, decided to go to the Prime Minister, and this they did on January 22. They proceeded to explain their position to the Prime Minister. They presented a brief, a copy of which I hold in my hand, and which could be summed up under these several heads: The brief stated, first, that the decontrol of non-scheduled air services was having very serious implications upon the industry; next, the lack of control was having a devastating effect upon the growth of the industry; commencing in 1958, with the decontrol of class C, the air industry met its first serious reversal; the real effect of the decontrol policy could not be evaluated until 1959 when a full year could be analysed, and this analysis, which had now been made, showed that

many, especially operators of long years' standing, will not be able to break even. It is alarming to note the number of carriers who have, in recent months, gone into bankruptcy. Unlimited competition in this field, the brief stated, is not necessary.
Then it went on to list its fears in connection with this decontrolling policy of the government which was opening up these groups B and C to full competition. It is stated that it is the considered opinion of the association that the continuance and/or extension of this policy can only create the following:
1.	A serious unemployment situation for skilled and dedicated personnel.
2.	Seasonal transportation, especially in specific areas.
3.	The possibility of discriminatory monopolies for certain outlying areas.
4.	A situation which will not only stifle but submerge a young, growing industry that has been one of the major factors in opening up the Canadian north and, lastly, a situation that could have a vital bearing on the safety of travel, more specifically to the Canadian north, with the obvious result of increased expenditures on search and rescue.
There is no doubt but that in the mind of the air industries transport association, in conference assembled, there was a great fear in the field of domestic aviation because of this decontrol policy. I will not go into that any further because there are a number of hon. members on this side of the house who will deal with it more appropriately than I can because they come from the outlying areas and they know how important it is that there should always be kept in mind by the governing and regulating bodies in this field the importance of safety in air travel.
The association, in its brief to the Prime Minister, concluded with these statements:
The association is fully satisfied that unrestricted licensing as a substitute for regulated competition will cause at least a deterioration in the service to the public and a serious setback to the industry with consequent delay in the development of the country.
It is our further opinion that unrestricted issue of licences cannot be construed as being in the best interest of the public, either from a convenience or a necessity point of view. Nor can it be construed as being in the best interests of the immediate or long term development of Canada as a whole.
3. We do not believe that there should be a restriction of free enterprise as it affects air transportation, but rather that competition should be regulated as provided for under the Aeronautics Act.
Of course in that last part of the brief they call upon the government for the formulation of a policy in this field as well as in other fields.
Civil Aviation
In recapitulation, Mr. Speaker, I state that the air industry is alarmed at the growing tendency to override the decisions of the air transport board. The board has a definite function to fulfil. The board is both an advisory and a judicial body. As such it has the right and, I say, the responsibility under the Aeronautics Act to hear applications that are made to it and to decide upon them upon the principle of public convenience and necessity. I say that the board has not been following that principle because it is being interfered with.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house a case in which there has been such interference. In doing so, I report it from an article which appeared in the Financial Post of November 7, 1959. I have reference, of course, to Autair Helicopter Services Limited of Montreal.
Autair Helicopter Limited. Montreal, was the first company to receive a class C helicopter licence after the minister's announcement.
That is the announcement which I have read made by the Minister of Transport in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
The licence was granted in July, 1958, after a hearing.
That was a very short time apparently after the statement made by the minister.
During the winter of 1958-59, Autair bought a fleet of 12 B-47J2 helicopters from Bell Helicopter Corporation, Fort Worth, Texas, bringing its whirly-bird total to 22.
Through most of 1959, Autair pushed other air transport operators out of the Quebec sky. The owner told Financial Post that his fleet was booked solid through October, 50 per cent by the Quebec government, 30 per cent by private industry and 20 per cent by the federal government.
But during the spring and summer, Autair ran into rough weather.
The company applied for permission to operate big helicopters.
In its application it said that its original licence was granted "as the result of revised government policy" rather than because it had shown "evidence of public convenience and necessity".
Autair asked that a restriction in its licence limiting the size of its helicopters be removed.
As it is required to do by the Aeronautics Act. A.T.B. fired back requests to Autair for financial and other information "in order to assist the board in forming an opinion as to whether it would be in the public interest to remove the restriction."
The company stood pat, provided no information. In June, A.T.B. considered the application on the evidence submitted at the original hearing, turned down the application. Autair promptly appealed to the minister.
At the end of August, the minister overruled A.T.B. on the application for removal of the restriction against big helicopters.
The company is now free to use them and it has never made any attempt to prove to A.T.B. that its big helicopter services are required "by public convenience and necessity".

speechtext: I hope the Minister of Public Works will reply to some of these matters. He thinks he is a smart minister and I am sure he knows everything about air. Perhaps he is going to reply to them. I had completed my statement on the Autair case-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-which apparently did not please the Minister of Public Works and I was going on to state that the air industries and transportation association complained about the manner in which that applications of this nature were granted. They did so, not only in their brief to the Prime Minister but also in a resolution which they passed at their annual meeting.
I should now like to say a word about the Aeronautics Act or the purpose of the Aeronautics Act and the functions of the air transport board which is established under the Aeronautics Act. First of all, I should like to put on Hansard the pertinent sections of the act which deal with applications of this nature. Section 15 of the Aeronautics Act, subsection 1 reads as follows:
Subject to the approval of the minister, the board may issue to any person applying therefor a licence to operate a commercial air service.
Subsection 3 of section 15 reads as follows:
The board shall not issue any such licence unless it is satisfied that the proposed commercial air service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity.
I say that the air transport board, in its determination of this case, decided against the application because of public convenience and necessity. I go a step further and say that the board, in exercising judicial functions, should not be overruled by the minister; in exercising advisory functions it can be overruled by the minister. My authority for that statement is a discussion which took place in this house when the former minister of munitions and supply, right hon. Mr. Howe, on June 6, 1944 introduced an amendment to the Aeronautics Act establishing the air transport board. I would like to put on Hansard the discussion, which was short, which took place between himself and the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Green) at that time, as reported on page 3604 of Hansard:
... This is a board which is both judicial and advisory.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In other words, the board of transport commissioners had to decide whether an applicant for a licence should get the licence, on certain well-defined principles, which might be summed up as public convenience and necessity, and it had also to follow certain judicial principles in deciding what tolls would be charged.
That is right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I understand it, this new transport board will no longer be subject to those

stipulations; it will no longer have to decide on the basis of public convenience and necessity whether or not a licence should be granted?
The jurisdiction is set out in the bill. I think if my hon. friend will delay this discussion until he sees the bill he will find that his fears in that regard are unnecessary.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But in effect now the minister is over and above that air transport board?
Not in judicial matters.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: While he was not over and above the board of transport commissioners? Is that not so?

I might point out that the board has two sets of functions. One is purely judicial; that is, when deciding matters of fact the board will be governed by the act; in that case the minister has no right to overrule them, except in the event of an appeal.
If I may interrupt, that is what I wanted to ask the minister. After the board has ruled on a judicial matter, is there a right of appeal to the minister or to some other body?

There is the right of appeal to the minister on certain matters, not all matters, but certain matters where there is an element of judgment as well as an element of judicial decision in interpreting the law. In certain limited matters there is provision for an appeal to the minister. Ordinarily, in judicial matters the board is bound by the act and its decision is final-
That is what was said on the occasion of the amendment to the Aeronautics Act establishing and setting up the air transport board, that it was a judicial body not subject to appeal in judicial matters.
So I come now to the conclusion of this part of my remarks. What is the policy of the government in respect to non-scheduled commercial air services? Is the board functioning as it should under the act? Are the board's functions going to be altered? Because if they are altered, in effect, by what the minister is doing, then the minister should come forward in this house and amend the Aeronautics Act, and not do it by a backdoor method by either a press release or an overruling of the air transport board.
The policy on civil air transport for Canada was carefully laid down in 1943 by the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King. It will be found at page 1776 et seq. of Hansard of April 2, 1943. I heard someone grunt as I mentioned the name of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King. I invite the grunter and those associated with him to read that policy, which is a clear-cut policy of the government of Canada in all fields of aviation. There has never been anything like it since then, and those of you who have been in office for the last three years who think that the time has now come because of technological or other changes to amend the policy, well, go ahead. We will listen to any changes you would like to make; but we on this side of the house ask you in all sincerity at least to make known what is your policy. Here is a clear-cut policy which I ask you
Civil Aviation
to read; it is summarized at the end. It deals with the international phase, the domestic phase and other phases of civil aviation. If my hon. friends would put their policy in a similar statement, then I think the country would be the better for it.
So I ask, what is the policy of the government in this field of aviation? We get it in an answer to a question which the hon. member for Vancouver South asked on two occasions. We get it in a press release. Surely that is not the way to enunciate policy. There must be a sound, sane, economically feasible air transport policy. This is desirable for all carriers. It is clear that the government has no such policy in these fields; it is making ad hoc decisions as and when the cases come up. There has been no policy laid down, as I said earlier, since that laid down by Mr. King in 1943.
What we do have though, in effect, is that the government is going too hard and too fast along the way of competition, and this notwithstanding the expert who was brought in by the government and whose recommendations appear in the Wheatcroft report, an expert from the United Kingdom who was asked to consider the whole field and who gave a clear definition of competition, namely that there should probably be in certain fields gradual competition. But at no place is it set out in this document that there should be all-out competition.
I say that in the fields I have mentioned so far there seems to be a tendency on the part of the government to favour all-out competition in-
Where?

To such traditional flying bogeys as ice and fog now must be added the name of a new hazard to aviation. Minister of Transport George Hees.

I now come to the third point in my remarks, namely the lack of policy in the field of air terminal construction. Here there has been-
