speechtext:
Then I should like to take a look at Canada's airports from one end of the country to the other. Apparently this is not being digested very easily by the Minister of Public Works who has a very important construction department, but who does not like this. Nor do some of his colleagues like it, because they have, in the same manner as we who sit on this side of the house, received very serious complaints about what is happening with regard to some of these terminals. For instance, I refer very briefly to the terminal at Patricia Bay where, according to an editorial which appeared in the

Victoria Times of December 8, 1959, the terminal building is "little more than a glorified chicken house."
Built by the Liberals.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Then a little later on, it says:
In the circumstances, Victorians cannot escape the unhappy feeling that the present federal government's disorderly financing is an impediment, perhaps insurmountable, to the creation of facilities pledged two years ago by the administration.
It looks to me as if there is more truth than poetry in that statement contained in this editorial of the Victoria Times. It looks to me as if the financial policy of the government is responsible for holding up work on a large number of these terminals in connection with which slow-down orders have been given.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Could I ask the hon. gentleman whether these particular terminals were not built under his own jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, these are terminals which were promised by the present administration, as the statement I have just read points out. The last paragraph reads:
Let us have the facts, good or bad. Let's hear details from our representatives in Ottawa. Their performance to date has not been encouraging.
That is a clear-cut statement of how that newspaper feels. Turning now to Winnipeg I note that the Winnipeg Tribune of December 3, 1959, contains this statement:
Announcement of a minimum five-year wait for a new airport terminal brought expressions of annoyance and disappointment today from Winnipeg and St. James representatives on the airport commission.
' It looks to me as if we will have to wait for the next election before we get any action", said St. James Mayor Thomas Findlay.
An article in the same paper on the same day, concludes with this paragraph:
If Prime Minister Diefenbaker cannot persuade Mr. Hees and the Department of Transport to give Winnipeg a modern airport building within two year:, he should fire the lot of them.
That is quite clear in its implications. Then:
There is no good reason why Winnipegers should not have a modern terminal within two years. The only real obstacle is the red tape, the indifference, and the do-it-next-year attitude in Ottawa.
There is also the question of Uplands. I ask the government: what is happening to the terminal at Uplands? Why is it necessary to wait such a long period of time in order to see this building completed and ready for operation?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Americans knocked it down.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My leader states that the Americans knocked it down. They shattered

the glass, but surely that would not take a whole year to replace. In addition, as the house knows, one has to taxi almost two miles before one gets from the air strip to the present terminal. Why is this project being held up for so long? Is the reason not the fact that it is being held up at treasury board because of a number of directives which have been given there?
I come now to one air terminal which is somewhat closer to me, and that is the Dorval air terminal. This is really a doozer, because if one examines it carefully there is nothing which can explain how over a period of three years little or nothing has been done by the present government to implement the completion of that air terminal. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, even if some of the delay were attributable to the previous administration-which I am not prepared to admit-here is the government which was going to set all these things right; here is the government which was going to straighten these things out and see to it that the buildings would be completed in no time. The Dorval airport is certainly a strange case, because the minister and his officials have made several contradictory statements about the terminal on more than one occasion. The minister, in an effort to stem the criticism directed against himself and the department decided to go to Montreal and invited the press to visit the airport. This was in November of 1959, and I have in my hand a clipping from the Montreal Gazette dealing with that affair. It begins:
Transport Minister Hees led a troupe of M.P.'s-*
Spelled with an "e".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, spelled with an "e". It says:
Transport Minister Hees led a troupe of M.P.'s and department officials to the partially-completed terminal at Montreal airport yesterday and said the new building would be ready next year-"as 1 always claimed it would be."
The present situation speaks for itself. Here is a press release No. 818, from the minister's office dated August 26, 1957. In fairness to the minister I must say that this statement was issued not by him but by his officers but I am sure he would not have allowed his officers to make this statement without clearing it himself. Here is what was said:
It is estimated that the building will near completion late in 1958 but it will take some months after that before installation of the complex operational equipment can be finished. Tentative opening date for the terminal is spring 1959.
The minister said it would be done in 1960 as "I have always claimed". In case the minister should disclaim this press release and
Civil Aviation
say he was not responsible for it-although I cannot see how he can do that in the face of the fact that it emanated from his own officers-I have another statement from the minister. This one was made at the dinner held in conjunction with the Canadian international air show at Toronto, Ontario, on Saturday, September 7, at 7.30 p.m.
What year?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no year marked on it. No date is given.
They just put it out every year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I had to busy myself and find out the date which gave me a lot of work and trouble. I eventually discovered that the year was 1957 as I can establish if anyone wants me to prove it.
On Saturday, September 7, 1957, the minister made this statement:
In two more years the demand for greatly increased airport facilities will be upon us. In these two years we must complete the construction of the six terminals now under way, namely, Ottawa, Montreal, Gander, St. John's, Windsor and Quebec city, and start construction on six to eight new terminals.
According to this statement the minister in 1957 was claiming that Dorval airport would be completed in two years, which would bring it to September 6, 1959. Here we are in the spring of 1960 and we are still waiting as I will show in a moment or two.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: On what date did the hon. member first announce the construction of Dorval airport?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will discuss that in a moment or two. I have a statement dealing with that which I will make in due course. I come to another statement which is contained in press release No. 818 concerning the final cost of the building. It reads:
Final cost of the building has been estimated at between $10 and $12 million.
The minister in his trip with the troupe of members of parliament on November 19, 1959, stated this:
Mr. Hees said the cost of the new facilities now would reach $30 million. As late as last year Mr. Hees said in the House of Commons that the cost of the project would be $15 million.
The question that occurs to my mind, naturally, in this. I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) is out of the house at this moment. Mind you, I am not complaining about the statement in so far as Dorval airport is concerned, but I

Civil Aviation
am complaining about the conduct and attitude of the Minister of Public Works on another occasion when he sought to sully the reputation of a predecessor of his, the Hon. Alphonse Fournier, in another place when he stated that the only statements before the committee were two items, one for $5 or $6 million for the construction of the printing bureau in Hull and another of $16 million representing the cost of the finished product. Where is the difference between what is being done now with respect to an airport which, according to the minister's own figures, has grown in cost from $10 million to $30 million as compared with a printing bureau growing in cost from $6 million to $16 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I answer that question, sir?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked a question.
Make your own speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the floor and I intend to keep it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Is the hon. member ashamed of himself?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the hon. member wants to reply-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member does not yield the floor the minister may not intervene.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister asked if I were ashamed of myself. I believe he should be ashamed of himself for trying to sully the reputation of one of his predecessors.
In connection with this airport, we do not have an over-all contract dealing with the whole business. The Minister of Public Works attempted in another place to say that this was contrary to good construction practice and contrary to the construction practice that exists in his department. Why does he not attempt to convince his colleague, the Minister of Transport, that this practice is not a proper one? If the practice was not the proper one to be followed in the other case, surely it is not the proper one here. Since this government has been in office it has continued in the last three years the practice of granting piecemeal contracts for the various parts of the building as they were given out from time to time.
With all respect, I say that what applied in a former case certainly applies in this case. I go further and say that if it is possible and easy in this case to see how we go from the original estimate in 1953 to the

present estimate in 1959, surely it would have been possible to do the same thing in the other case. But, oh no, there was just one tendency, one attitude, and one object in those days and that was to destroy those who happened to sit on the other side of the house.
A moment ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) asked me when I had announced the building of the airport at Dorval. I have no hesitation in saying that it was in 1953. I stated at that time that the cost of the construction of the Dorval airport terminal would be $4 million. The next year my successor, Mr. Marler, announced amended plans for the building and work commenced in that year.
I am not complaining that what is being done at Dorval concerning additions is not being properly done. What I am complaining about is that a similar circumstance existed elsewhere and there were serious complaints made by hon. gentlemen opposite but no complaint has been made by the present government in connection with this circumstance and certainly no complaint has been made by the Minister of Public Works to his colleague the Minister of Transport so far as I know. Here we are in early 1960 and the building at Dorval airport is not only far from completion but, from the information I have, there are still some contracts to be awarded.
In an attempt to stem the criticism the minister made the visit which I mentioned earlier in my remarks. I should like here to quote a paragraph from an article in the Montreal Gazette of November 19, 1959, which I am sure will strike the house as being somewhat peculiar:
Those who accompanied the official party-the minister, the deputy minister, the chief architect, the chief engineer-and the M.P.'s on the tour were struck by the few workmen visible on any of the floors.
In fact, I am informed that there were not more than 25 workers at the airport at that time. I am told that the position is exactly the same today.
As reported in La Presse on March 1, 1960, at a meeting of the administrators of the unemployment insurance commission in Montreal in the presence of the regional director, the president of the Montreal labour council made the following statement:
(Translation):
Mr. Louis Laberge, chairman of the Montreal labour council, who introduced the resolution, stated that the government, which verbally supports the winter works campaign, should set the example. He stated, however, that the works carried out by the government at Dorval airport and at central station are practically at a standstill this winter.

(Text):
There we have the statement made by a Montreal labour official on March 1, 1960 that there are few workmen on the job. In the light of that situation, how is it possible to hasten the completion of the terminal? I go further and say that engineers who are familiar with the project state that it cannot possibly be completed before 1961. If that is the case, it will be eight years after the first announcement was made in the house. Meanwhile the present premises are left far behind the constant growth in traffic. The press, the Montreal tourist bureau and many others have drawn attention to the delays in the construction of the air terminal as well as to the very grave harm being done Montreal as an international airport. The Minister of Transport says there is no delay and he stated in the house that the work was going full speed ahead.
Next month T.C.A. will launch its new 125 passenger jets. If and when several flights of this character arrive at the same time the overcrowding will be intolerable. What are the reasons for the delay? Some are due to technical developments which brought about changes in plans. Others may be laid squarely at the door of treasury board. During consideration of the minister's estimates last year we were told in the house that treasury board now requires to be given detailed economic studies at the time any additional expenditures are recommended so that the board will get a comprehensive idea of the whole picture. But surely these studies should not take a matter of years.
Additional expenditures required the approval of treasury board after the Conservatives took office. They have been in office for three years. Is treasury board still studying these expenditures after that time? Are we in Montreal to wait until 1961 before the building is open to the public? Are enough men employed on the job to ensure that the work will go ahead satisfactorily? Is the governments financial position such that contracts are being held up for financial reasons? Has a slow-down order been issued with respect to all terminal buildings in the same manner as seems to have been done on other projects? Is the development of the aeroquay a further cause of delay? These are questions which I think should be answered before the debate is over.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Can my friend answer who suggested the architects for the enterprise?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What has that got to do with it? Many architects were suggested by the
Civil Aviation
former government and there have been the same delays, not only here but at other airports. I say that the cause of the delay is that the government in its anxiety and desire to balance its budget at any cost is holding up these terminals from one end of the country to the other.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What held them up before?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There was no hold-up before. You and your followers have been in office for three years. What have you done? Surely you should have shown some progress during the time you have been in office. In an attempt to be helpful I have made a suggestion to the minister and I make it here in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: When he is not here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why isn't he?
Why isn't he here?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is the second time the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker! has brought that up and I repeat that it is the responsibility of every minister to be in his place in the house during the debate on an amendment to go into supply because on such an occasion any matter may be discussed which affects any department. If the minister is not here certainly it is not the fault of the one who is moving the amendment. The suggestion I made on that occasion was the following, that a committee should be established at once, being responsible to the minister and composed of representatives of the Department of Transport, the air lines, contractors, architects and treasury board, whose duties would be to inquire into (1) the reasons for the delay in the completion of the terminal building and the fact that the building may not be completed before 1961; (2) recommendation of ways and means of co-ordinating the actions of these five interested groups so that the building will be completed and ready for operation without further delay; and (3) the implementation of these recommendations.
I did receive a letter from the minister in answer to my suggestion in which he gave reasons why my recommendation could not be accepted. I am still of the view that if that recommendation had been accepted we would be further advanced today than we are. Such a procedure has been followed on other occasions and it proved satisfactory and successful. To back up what I have said earlier, I look at the estimates of the Department of Transport and I find that so far as the airport program is concerned, they have been cut by $11 million. Again I ask, is the government cutting down on airports, air

Civil Aviation
terminals and airport construction in a feverish desire to balance the budget at any cost?
I think the time has arrived to give consideration to the amount of criticism in the city of Montreal in connection with this matter. There is not one newspaper that has not been highly critical of the officials of the government. It is not so much the officials of the Department of Transport who should be criticized as those of treasury board who have been cutting down these estimates, who have been holding them up, who have been making investigations to ascertain whether these expenditures were required. The most stinging rebuke to the government was that contained in an editorial in La Presse in which the question was posed whether or not this was not discrimination on the part of the government against the international airport of Montreal, against the construction of the air terminal and with respect to the position so far as the disgraceful terminal now in use is concerned.
So I say without hesitation that the government by its lack of policies has (1) given away our sovereignty in the air by granting foreign air lines onward privileges which Canada itself does not possess; (2) done untold harm to small operators in the field of non-scheduled air services by its policy of all-out competition; and, (3) created complete chaos in the construction of main airport terminals. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets the shortsighted and irresponsible policy of the government in the field of civil aviation which has been characterized by:
1.	The giving up of Canadian sovereign rights in the air without obtaining similar rights in return;
2.	Discrimination against small air lines providing services especially in the outlying areas of Canada;
3.	Uncertainty and delay in the construction of air terminal facilities.

Would the hon. member
permit a question before he resumes his seat?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

I think the hon. member said that the amount of money available for the construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment had gone down, but according to the book of estimates I have here, in 1958-59 it was $61 million, and it is now up to $63 million in the current estimates.
This is a statement, not a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not ask a question, he made a statement.
I say, how do you get a reduction?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The reduction in estimates for airport construction is $11 million.
It is still $63 million.

Mr. Speaker, my party can support almost everything said in the tour de force we have just heard from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). We certainly support the amendment wholeheartedly. A question that has bothered me for two or three years now has been the very peculiar myth that has grown up about the Department of Transport to the effect that, at last, the department is in the hands of an able, hard-hitting person who is getting things done. My own personal opinion is that this is one department that is in as poor shape as the poorest. I think the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Laurier have gone a considerable way toward highlighting this.
It seems to me that the minister in charge of this department entered his job with some unique idea about free enterprise; what he was going to do was to bring the breath of free enterprise into his particular scope of operation in this department. Three years later we find that the free enterprise may be there, but it seems to me we are reaping the results of a completely inadequate policy.
One of the difficulties in following someone who has had the amount of time that the hon. member for Laurier had is that you discover that item after item which you were prepared to use has already been put forward. I thought perhaps the most striking of all the evidence that was used by the hon. member for Laurier was the brief from the air industries and transport association of Canada. This brief, which was sent around to all members in January, is one of the most stinging rebukes that could be given by a public association. When I say "public association", I mean an association that draws its membership from many, many organizations in the field. This brief contains one of the most bitter attacks upon this government that I have seen. I think the point that I should like to emphasize most is point 3 which is set forth on page 3 of the brief. It reads:
We do not believe that there should be a restriction of free enterprise as it affects air transportion, but rather that competition should be regulated as provided for under the Aeronautics Act.
In other words, the minister, through his policy has been ignoring the Aeronautics Act. I thought the hon. member for Laurier brought that out very well. The peculiar thing about air transportation, as it has been in all transport services in Canada, has been

this continuous demand for the cutting back of public operations or public corporations in this field to make way for free enterprise. At the same time it seems to me there is a failure to realize the enormous cost to the taxpayers of the nation as a whole in the provision of the basic services that enable these private enterprises to operate. We can see this trend in the railway industry because, at this particular year, there is still a controversy over the Crowsnest pass rates which resulted from the legacy or bounty of some of the gifts that were given in the past to the Canadian Pacific railway.
We have this same or similar phase introduced by this particular government with the opening up of the transcontinental air privileges, in a limited form, to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I wonder whether hon. members, and the people as a whole, realize just how much the provision of the basic services that enable air lines to operate cost the taxpayers of this country. We have to have these kinds of services because, aside from moving people and goods, they fit in with our defence picture, our weather picture and other services the people need. Surely the very enormity of the expenditures indicates that this whole question of free competition, free enterprise, is a silly one in this field, and that the provisions of the Aeronautics Act, with its rather strict regulations, are rather good. These provisions have been denied by the policies of this particular government, with regard to its failure to bring in any changes in the act and, as the hon. member for Laurier pointed out very well, there has been a complete failure to tell us what their policy may be.
In my opinion, one of the ironies about this particular minister-I regret he is not here-is that one of his favourite themes when he was in opposition-I do not like bringing up what people said when they were in opposition because I know their habits and their manners change when they get into government-was that the civil service was too large. He thought the civil service was growing too big, there was too much fat in it and it could be cut down. The irony is that he has the fastest growing department in the government. I notice that in the department's annual report, which came out within the last two days, for the first time in many years they have discontinued giving the number of employees in this department. The last annual report contained a chart showing the number of employees and how rapidly the number was growing. However, that chart has disappeared from this year's annual report.
One of the main branches in which this growth is taking place in the Department of 79951-0-114
Civil Aviation
Transport is that branch concerned with the provision of these services for air lines.
If we had socialism we would all be in a department of some sort.

That is the very point with which I wanted to deal. Socialists are always accused of wanting to increase the size of government departments. All I can say is that this free enterpriser we have at the head of the ministry of transport is doing a very good job of it. I am sure the Minister of Labour must be grateful for the efforts of the Department of Transport in trying to take up the unemployment slack, because here is a department that is growing at a fantastic rate in terms of employees and in terms of the amount of money that is being spent. If you check the last annual report and look at the summary of expenditures and revenue you will find this striking point, that expenditures for air services in the fiscal year 1958-59 have reached the fantastic total of $115 million, whereas the revenues we got were only $11 million. There is over $100 million difference between revenues and expenditures.
When a government department or a branch of a government department reaches this size, we need to take a very close look at it. When their revenues are so far below their expenditures, I wonder why we find even this government is bringing in free enterprise in so far as these continental routes are concerned. It is threatening to put a great corporation that was and has been on a paying basis into a deficit position. I certainly agree that the evidence of the order in council submitted by the hon. member for Laurier indicates that the future of Trans-Canada Air Lines is rather bleak indeed. He made the point that it is bleak because of the give-away program of the minister in relation to international air routes. I think we could perhaps say a bigger reason has been the domestic giveaway to Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
One of the reasons why these fantastic expenditures are going to skyrocket is, of course, the introduction of the very large jets. I have not enough technical understanding to appreciate just what has to be provided but from people who are involved in the transport business I know that we are not ready in Canada either in terms of runways, terminals, navigational facilities or even our meteorological system, for highspeed jet travel. This means that this particular minister is going to keep coming into the house, as long as this government is in power, asking for increased expenditures in order to provide these facilities. It is also obvious, just from a statement of revenue- it is a pittance, being one eleventh of the total expenditures-that we are not going to

Civil Aviation
get a decent return from any revenues that we can charge for the use of these facilities.
My point-and I want to reiterate it-is that in the provision of air transport, commercial transport in particular, there is on the part of the taxpayer a subsidization that is tremendous. Our point in this particular party is that in a field where you have such a basic subsidization, this free enterprise or competitive concept is a nonsensical one and that what you need is a regulatory body'- which we have-and a plan that will allow competition where it is at all possible or feasible but at least the kind of competition that does not dynamite the stability that the particular commercial services were building up. That is the gist of the criticism made by the air industries and transport association of Canada. I am delighted to find that this group of free enterprisers is prepared to stand up and be counted on the silliness of the free enterprise idea running wild.
One of the facts that faces Trans-Canada Air Lines is, of course, the tremendous amount of money it has had to put out in order to enter the jet field. We can see an end to a certain extent of the jet race in so far as commercial airliners are concerned. An expert in this field told me the other day he expects there will be only one more shift from the jets that are presently coming into service to another form of jet before we shall have reached the ceiling of that particular kind of transportation. He expected this ceiling would be reached about the end of this decade.
What is the expert's name?

Civil Aviation
kind of union and pooling advocated by Mr. Davoud. In the light of the kind of services we want and need I think we must look toward co-operation and pooling, not more competition.
I was interested to note that in the report of the air transport board to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) on trans-continental air services the board went very thoroughly into this whole competition aspect. I would like to read what I think is the key paragraph so far as this is the kind of opinion which seems to have influenced the minister and the government. I refer to page 8 of this particular report:
The board has considered the various views expressed and has reached the following conclusions :
1.	On the part of many members of the public there are no strong views for or against transcontinental air competition;
I think that is very true.
2.	On the part of those members of the public who have interested themselves in these proceedings, the majority opinion favours transcontinental competition for reasons of personal or business convenience, some expressing this view irrespective of the cost thereof either to the taxpayers or to any private carrier, while some felt such competition should only be permitted if shown to be economically feasible.
Mr. Speaker, we will soon know whether the competition was economically feasible when we see the Trans-Canada Air Lines annual report. It seems to me that this government-I think this has influenced a number of government supporters, and I think especially of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) who is a bit of an expert in air management-has been inordinately influenced by the opinion that Canadians want transcontinental competition to suit their business convenience and, if I might just paraphrase, hang the cost either to the taxpayer or the public corporation which we have in existence. There are stages and areas of transportation where competition is an expensive luxury.
The third point that the hon. member for Laurier Stressed, using particularly the example of Dorval, was the uncertainty and delay in the construction of air terminal facilities. He pointed out, very properly, that this particular year, despite the forecast made a couple of years ago that there were six airports to be completed and six new ones to be launched, the government has slashed its estimates. I see that the Department of Transport estimates have been slashed by a total of $17 million for air services for the fiscal year ahead of us. In light of the steady growth of the air services so far as personnel and administration is concerned, it is very

apparent that much of this slash must lie in the expansion of the existing facilities.
This particular slash, it seems to me, is most unfortunate in the light of the kind of criticism that we are hearing from the present air lines. I would like to refer to an article in the Financial Post of December 12, 1959 headed, "Air lines boil over out-dated air terminals". It is an article by Mr. Baxter, and he goes on to say:
Airlines serving Canada are coming to a boil over our air terminal situation.
On the eve of the jet age in Canada, they feel our terminals are still in the biplane era.
They blame the Department of Transport and its planners. D.O.T. replies that its policy (slow and careful) is the right one.
I do not know whether that slow and careful policy happens to have been the right one, but there is no question that this department is now slowing down on terminal development if we look at the estimates.
One of the things that occurs to me in connection with air line terminals and their cost is, of course, the shifts that are taking place in international traffic. The hon. member for Laurier mentioned the airport at Gander. I think any of us who have seen the magnificent terminal facilities there will recognize that they are, excellent-that they are up to world standards. I have gathered, though, that there has been a continuing drop in the amount of use that is being made of Gander and that in future, with the wider use of jet aircraft, traffic through Gander will continue to fall both in terms of landings and in terms of revenue. We know that this government is putting a considerable amount of money into Frobisher airport and I hear, also, that the use made of Frobisher is likely to decline. I mention these particular cases to suggest that far more emphasis should perhaps be given to the airports which are properly in Canada and within the areas of large population or serving middle-sized cities. I am thinking especially of Dorval, Malton and the facilities at Winnipeg.
This party feels that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Laurier is somewhat inadequate in that it does not cover several points which we think should be brought up in criticism of the present government as far as its air policy is concerned. We think the hon. gentleman has done a striking job in outlining the complete lack of policy of the Minister of Transport in this particular field, but we think there are several other points which should be mentioned. I have referred to one of them, and that is the unnecessary duplication of domestic transcontinental services introduced a year ago, which

gives every indication of severely undermining the profit position, efficiency and wellbeing of Trans-Canada Air Lines. We think the government has given no indication that it is really aware of the kind of planning which is going to be necessary with regard to international arrangements of all kinds.
I notice that in the most recent annual report of the minister there is a note on page 7 which says that a new directorate was planned in order to co-ordinate the programming of all future major air service projects. This indicates that the department at least has some ideas, but it was my contention last year, and it will be in the future, that this department is now too big for one minister. It is too big for one deputy minister, and I think the topic upon which we are engaged today has reached the stage, especially in terms of expenditure, when a minister should be in charge of this increasingly important branch of transportation. I do not see how we can in all conscience continue the situation which exists at present, where the Secretary of State, whose functions really amount to nothing at all- pardon me, the Solicitor General-
You were close.

The Secretary of State does have a few more functions. The Solicitor General has a cabinet post and a cabinet salary, and does very little. Yet here we have this huge branch which is sprawling across the country, growing at a fantastic rate, and costing well over $100 million a year. Yet it shares the attention of one minister who is struggling with this task and not doing a very good job of it, as the criticisms made today have indicated. I think this is a field for which a cabinet minister should certainly be made responsible.
In that event, the whole question of air services might receive the kind of attention and long range planning that this country needs because, despite the strictures I have made concerning the cost to the taxpayer of these projects, they are projects which are necessary and worth while if the expansion to which we look forward in this field is to take place. This expansion has to take place, however, within a rational framework. If the air industry can bring to the attention of the government criticism such as it makes in the brief which is now available to us, it is surely time for the government to admit that it has not a policy of any kind.
I should like to re-emphasize that we feel that as part of its policy the government should support the domestic air industry. This particular document is a brief from the Canadian aircraft industry submitted to the
Civil Aviation
government of Canada by the united automobile workers of America in co-operation with the Canadian Labour Congress. I must say that there are parts of this pamphlet with which I cannot agree. The intention of this brief is, or was, of course, to keep the Arrow in production. It was produced shortly before the present government decided to discontinue the Arrow program. Now that this decision has been made there will be no going back to Canadian production in that field. Neither can I see how we can plan to provide from within our own aircraft industry the supersonic air liners, or the big jet air liners which are now going into service. It seems to me that the kinds of aircraft upon which we should concentrate are the planes and helicopters that we shall be using in Canada for most of our feeder lines and the development of the north, for example, the Beaver and the Cariboo, whose success has already been sufficient to indicate that concentration in this field, with government leadership and encouragement, could provide us not only with a home market but also with a world market for aircraft of this type. The production of these aircraft by Canadian industry might need as much subsidization as has been necessary in the past.
For all these reasons, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), that the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following:
(4)	Unnecessary duplication of domestic transcontinental airlines services which has denied Trans-Canada Air Lines the opportunity to implement further reduction in fares;
(5)	Lack of planning necessary to assure Canadians the international and domestic air services required to meet the needs of the future;
(6)	Failure to maintain and promote a stable domestic aircraft industry.

Mr. Speaker, I followed with great interest the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) which, I believe, could be summed up in the two words "sour grapes". I should like to take issue with the hon. member, particularly with regard to the subject of airport construction and allied facilities. The figures, which were repeated by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) do not appear to me to be correct. I have here the estimates for the year 1959 and the year 1960.
I wonder if the hon. member knows that I was using the estimates for the next year, 1960-61?

Yes, I understood that. The estimates for 1957-58 showed an appropriation for the acquisition of land and the construction of buildings, and so on, of some $35 million. The estimates for 1958-59 showed an increase of $26 million making a total of

Civil Aviation
$61 million. The estimates for 1959-60 indicate a total of $63 million. That is a fair indication of the importance this government attaches to the question of air transportation in Canada and to the building of facilities that will handle the air traffic that is engendered.
The hon. member for Laurier spoke at great length about what he called the lack of construction of proper airport facilities and he spoke particularly about terminals. I should like to remind the hon. gentleman that the advent of the jet age has brought problems compared with which the problem of terminal facilities is minor. Of equal or more significance are the problems of landing strips, length of runways, etc. For instance, the relocation of the airport at Edmonton in terms of present day costs might well be considered to be equal to the cost of the construction of all airport facilities in Canada that were built up to about ten years ago. I know that in my native city of Vancouver the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has been trying to come to an agreement with the city fathers for the construction there of an air terminal that will be worthy of the city and the present day and increased future air traffic which it will be required to handle.
I was interested in the hon. member for Laurier reading out a list of the airports under construction. Some of these have come to my attention in my own travels across Canada. I have seen the new airport under construction at Edmonton and the new municipal airport at Calgary. There is also the proposed new airport at Winnipeg. When the hon. member was referring to that airport I had an opportunity to check with the construction people in the Department of Transport who advised me that the tenders for the first stage of the construction of that airport are before treasury board now and should be through this week.
We appreciate that what is taking place at 1 urval is taking place rather slowly but we oi>.,erved no great speed under the regime of the Liberals when according to the hon. member's own admission the project was announced in 1953 and had not been accomplished up to the time this government took office. New airport facilities are proposed at Toronto.
All of these projects are in the estimates that appear in the blue book. Anybody can refer to them and in doing so should understand that they reflect a program of expansion and activity that certainly was not matched by the previous administration. When in one year the estimates relating to construction are practically doubled this is a good indication of the recognition of this government of the need for facilities across Canada. If one were to go back

into the estimates a few years ago I suspect one would find that the amount expended on airports was just a matter of a few million dollars.
I am particularly concerned about the remarks made concerning competition. I am familiar with the attitude taken by the former government of which the hon. member for Laurier was so distinguished a member for so long a time. The attitude of his government was one under which Canadian Pacific Air Lines which pioneered the route from Vancouver to Amsterdam and flew the polar route were not allowed landing privileges at Edmonton. If a passenger from Edmonton wanted to go to Amsterdam he was required to travel from Edmonton to Vancouver. Then the Liberal government made its wonderful concession under which it allowed C.P.A. to come down at Yellowknife. The hon. member for Laurier made quite a play on the word Bangkok but I suggest that an equal play could be made on the word Yellowknife. Passengers from Edmonton were then required to travel to Yellowknife to pick up this plane. Of course, the people of Edmonton saw the plane flying overhead every night but it was not allowed to land there. Initially they had to go to Vancouver to board the plane but under the special dispensation given by Mr. Howe they were allowed to board it at Yellowknife.
I also remember the stand the Liberal government took in regard to Eastern Air Lines a few years ago in respect of its run from Montreal to New York city. Finally the government had the courage to say, "If you do not withdraw your objection to landing rights at New York we will take away yours at Montreal."
The hon. member for Laurier had the nerve to get up and list the routes he says we have given away without receiving consideration. He mentioned B.O.A.C. and the pooling of facilities with T.C.A. and said the only people to benefit would be B.O.A.C., that the use by each company of the other's facilities would be of no benefit whatever to T.C.A. I suggest that that is the attitude which was taken by the former administration which was reflected throughout the entire speech the hon. member made. That attitude is one under which we have one favourite child and there shall be no competition for that child, and that child may do what it wants.
I am as strong a supporter and admirer of the operations of T.C.A. as is the hon. member for Laurier, but I will not go as far as he goes in that respect because I have travelled on air lines over the years and have seen

what competition has done by way of improvements and services not only in the air but on the ground. I believe competition is good for T.C.A.
In the report on air line competition in Canada which I hold in my hand it is stated that the most profitable routes are transAtlantic and southern. Where do we find the greatest competition? On the trans-Atlantic run.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
