Mr. Speaker, I have noticed on looking at Hansard for Friday that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) expressed some surprise at that time that anyone should debate this bill. I have not had time to look up the exact words but I think he said that in the 15 years he had been a member of parliament he had never known one of these bills to be debated. Of course, the minister did not contend, and I am not suggesting that he did, that the motion was not debatable. It is debatable. But I agree with the minister that it is a very unusual thing to debate an interim supply bill, particularly if there has been a protracted debate, as there was, on the estimates themselves, and I make no apology for my part in it.
I would not have ventured to take up time which belongs to the opposition anyway on a supply day to say anything about this matter if it had not been for the rather extraordinary circumstances associated with the supplementary estimates that are now embodied in the supply bill. The other day one of our colleagues in the house took some exception to technicalities. I, sir, make no apology for observing technicalities because it is the technicalities in our rules, as the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Eglinton, will remember, that not very many years ago were used a good deal on this side of the house by certain hon. gentlemen who are now on the treasury benches.
But it is not in any sense because of technicalities that I want to say the few things I wish to say today. I do think that since the
Appropriation Act
present government was elected there has been no more shocking example of contempt for the most fundamental rights of parliament than was shown by the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) on the estimates in committee of supply when an emergency item for which he was responsible was debated.
You talked on them for eight days.
I think the hon. member was perhaps asleep for most of those eight days because-
If I was asleep it was because there was nothing worth listening to.
I think the hon. member for Victoria has characterized his own contributions to the house very well in the last three words.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Be careful which Victoria you refer to.

The hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia. I know the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hodgson) is so busy preparing the speech he is going to make later this evening that he should not be interrupting me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) is going to do that.

The most fundamental of all rights of parliament is the right to determine what levies will be imposed upon the taxpayers and to determine how those moneys that are collected from the taxpayers will be spent. I do not think it would be appropriate at this stage to go into it again but we did take considerable exception to the way in which this whole matter was proceeded with. Even on the basis of the way in which it was proceeded with we were told some very extraordinary things by the Minister of Agriculture.
You are doublecrossing the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcll-raith).

In the course of the debate on this item the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and myself pressed the minister very strongly to tell us how this money was going to be spent. I am addressing my remarks now particularly to the Minister of Finance who, I regret to say, was not in the house at the time this exchange took place because, if he had been, I would have asked the questions of him right there and then instead of taking the time of the house now. We insisted that the committee of supply was entitled to be told the scheme

Appropriation Act
under which this money was being paid out. I am not going to give the quotations unless I am asked to give them but the minister suggested that would have been a dictatorial attitude on the part of the government, an authoritarian attitude. I say, sir, as I said then, that it is wholly improper for the Minister of Finance, who has the ultimate responsibility to the house in this matter, to be paying out money without knowing what the ultimate destination of that money is. Here is what the Minister of Agriculture finally told us after repeated pressure with respect to what he knew about how this money was being spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: What date is that?

February 9, and it will be found at page 899 of Hansard. He said:
As far as the actual details of the schemes put into effect in the three provinces are concerned, the information which I received from the provinces was in the form of press releases which they put out in each case. It just so happens I have not got them with me at the moment, but I have sent for them and expect them to be here in a few minutes.
I raised the question whether the Minister of Finance, who boasted about the care and precision with which he had gone over all these estimates, and treasury board had been satisfied with press releases which the Minister of Agriculture did not even bother bringing into the committee when he was trying to get us to vote this money, if the minister was satisfied if that was all the scrutiny that treasury board was giving to the payment of public money, and I got no answer to that whatsoever. As I say, if the Minister of Finance had been present at the time I would have asked him the questions I am asking now and to which I hope he will reply before this debate concludes. As the Minister of Finance well knows, though the Minister of Agriculture did not seem to know it, in all the other schemes for sharing expenditures where the province actually pays out the money there are the most careful provisions for audit and the most careful conditions laid down as to how these payments shall be made, to whom and under what circumstances.
I have no doubt that all three provincial governments are carrying out their responsibilities properly. I do not wish to reflect upon them in any way. But our duty is to the people that we were elected to represent and it is our duty as members of the house not to vote money on the basis of press releases issued by provincial governments. We have a right to know and, indeed, we have the duty to find out precisely what these schemes are and how the money is

paid out. I feel that before the supply bill passes the Minister of Finance should give us in detail the scheme under which these payments are made.
The other thing that made this matter all the more shocking was the fact that, over and over again all through the debate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River kept pressing the Minister of Agriculture to explain how certain procedures were being carried out in the province of Manitoba. He asked repeatedly about the use of officials of the P.F.R.A. by the provincial government for certain purposes. It was absolutely impossible to get any satisfactory explanation from the minister, who took a Pontius Pilate attitude about the whole thing, and said this was none of the business of the federal government and refused to provide the information.
During all that time, as we found out from a return which was made after repeated requests on my part, several days after the item had passed-the correspondence with Saskatchewan and Alberta, as hon. members will recall was brought down during the course of the debate but the correspondence with Manitoba was not-that on January 20, the minister of agriculture for Manitoba had written a letter to the Minister of Agriculture here in Ottawa about this very matter about which my hon. friend was asking the minister. The minister had this letter, unanswered, all the time and we were denied the information here. He had a lot more than this press release. I could read this letter now, but I do not want to take up a lot of time.
You are doublecrossing the hon. member for Ottawa West.

I have no doubt the hon. member for Ottawa West is able to defend himself and will be able to do so without any help from that voice from the far west.
I draw your attention to the reply which the Minister of Agriculture made to the minister of agriculture for Manitoba. This reply is dated February 10. The item passed on February 9, and the minister replied on February 10. Here is what he said:
Ottawa, February 10, 1960 The Hon. George Hutton,
Minister of Agriculture and Conservation, Province of Manitoba,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Dear Mr. Hutton,
In reply to your letter of January 20, I have now had time to consider further your request-
This was a request with respect to this matter that we were debating in this house. The minister would not deign to give us

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
any information, but as soon as the item passed, the next morning he went into his office and wrote this letter.
In reply to your letter of January 20, I have now had time to consider further your request, and that of the other two ministers of agriculture for the prairie provinces, that the dominion government pay 50 per cent of the administrative costs, rather than making the payments previously proposed to the municipalities to cover part of the cost of administration.
We were told none of these details. The next paragraph reads:
My colleagues have agreed to meet this request, and we will be prepared to pay 50 per cent of your administration expenses, as approved by our treasury officials.
The third paragraph is the one I wish particularly to outline because this seems to me to be the epitome of this outrage to parliament.
You are probably aware that the vote to cover the dominion government's share of the assistance payments was passed in the House of Commons yesterday. I expect it will go through the Senate shortly and we will then be in a position to make payments to you.
I say that it was an absolutely outrageous thing for the minister, with that letter of January 20 before him, with the repeated requests from us who have the responsibility for voting this money for the purposes referred to in that letter, to deny this information to the committee, to deny the committee the correspondence, and then to write a letter like that in obvious contempt of this house immediately after the item had passed. It is because of that that I feel impelled to take a little time of the house today to stress the fact that we on this side of the house do believe we have a duty to uphold the rights of parliament. I know from reading the public prints, that when we seek to uphold our rights, we are attacked by no less a person than the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The Prime Minister is reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 8 as having said at a dinner on February 6 that the Liberals had a new policy of personal attacks on his government. I have no doubt that the suggestion the Minister of Agriculture should give this committee the information to which it is entitled will now be described as a personal attack on that gentleman. But it is nothing of the kind, any more than any attacks which were made upon the Prime Minister were personal attacks. No one on this side, I know, has attacked the Prime Minister or any other minister for anything except their failure to perform their duties in the fashion we believe they should be performed. Surely if an opposition has any duty that is a duty of the opposition.
Since I resolved to make these observations another matter has cropped up and I want 79951-0-115
Appropriation Act
to say a word about that. We had, as we were reminded, on eight different days- which is a very different thing from saying it was an eight-day debate-a debate about the winter works program, an item which we also find embodied in the bill before us. The Prime Minister did not see fit to take any part in that debate. The debate concluded at six o'clock on March 3. Within two hours, the Prime Minister went on television, and I have in my hand a transcript of what the Prime Minister said. I want to read a little bit from that transcript into the record because this is what the Prime Minister had to say on this matter of unemployment which we were debating, on the program entitled "The Nation's Business".
And as you know, there was the unemployment problem which we inherited. I don't want to see a single day of unnecessary suffering.
"Unnecessary suffering", I draw your attention to those words.
Neither do my colleagues. And the result was we had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to provide jobs through housing and public works and other projects. We have planned for a deficit. We had to borrow money. We were, of course, criticized for this, but when I thought of the families of the unemployed, I knew for me there was no other course, deficit or no deficit. In the same circumstances, I would make exactly the same decision again.
Now, sir, those words were-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Would my hon. friend just read the quote, because we do not want to go each time from the sublime to the ridiculous.

The Minister of Public
Works (Mr. Walker), who was publicly rebuked by the Speaker this afternoon, would be well advised not to court another public rebuke this evening, because in my recollection during the 20 years I have been in Ottawa, this is the first time a Speaker has found it necessary to rebuke a member of the treasury benches. I asked myself, as I heard that rebuke, if the appointment of the minister to the cabinet was the reason-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member who has the floor is straying a bit from the theme.

I quite appreciate that, and I do not feel I should demean myself by straying any further from the field in the particular direction in which I was going. Perhaps if the Minister of Public Works could contain himself until I have concluded my speech, then I would be glad to listen politely to any contribution he has to make. I have read what the Prime Minister said about unemployment during this broadcast which was made within two hours of the debate being concluded in the committee of supply.

Appropriation Act
We know the level of unemployment in this year 1960 and in this month of March, or at least we know something about the level of February, although we have not yet the figures for March. We know that the level of unemployment is unhappily, notwithstanding the buoyancy of the economy in other respects, nearly as great as it was two years ago. We know also that all the government is doing about it at the present time is embodied in one of the items in this bill providing $15 million for the winter works program. We have parliament doing the one thing and then within two hours we have the Prime Minister of this country saying this:
We were, ol course, criticized for this, but when I thought of the families of the unemployed. I knew for me there was no other course, deficit or no deficit. In the same circumstances, I would make exactly the same decision again.
It is perfectly obvious that the government has not in the same circumstances made the same decision or any similar decision at all. But there is another very remarkable thing about what the Prime Minister said. We all remember what he said over and over again all over this country in the election campaign two years ago. I will just quote one of these references. It is from a telecast on February 18, 1958. It is in an item from the Montreal Star and it reads as follows:
On the live telecast Mr. Diefenbaker said he would take any practical step to ease unemployment in addition to his billion dollar public works plan.
That is one of the many visions that have vanished.
Unemployment reached a post-war record of 520,000 in mid-January.
What was the situation in January, 1960? The lowest figure was 504,000.
So when I said there was very little difference, despite the buoyancy of the economy, between the two situations, I was not exaggerating. Then the Prime Minister said this and this is in quotation marks:
"As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada," he said in a live telecast, "everything that can be done-everything without regard to the limit-[DOT] will be done to the end that no one will suffer."
Oh, yes; that was in 1958 before an election. What is it in 1960, two years after the election, with almost the same level of unemployment? It is this:
I don't want to see a single day of unnecessary suffering.
In 1958 he said that no one will suffer. In 1960, what does the Prime Minister say about employment? He says: not necessarily suffering, but suffering if necessary.
Oh, oh.

That is the change in two years: not necessarily suffering but all the necessary suffering over and above $15 million. That is the remarkable change in two years. Yet I read in the Montreal Gazette this very self-regarding praise by the hon. gentleman who is the Associate Minister of National Defence-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: He is not here.
No; it is very extraordinary how few of these ministers ever are in this house, as the Minister of Public Works is so fond of bringing to our attention.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Where is your party today?

The associate minister was quoted as saying this:
"With the present government," Mr. Sevigny said, "national unity is an accomplished fact, our leaders do not promise one thing in one area and promise the opposite somewhere else. Our leaders have made the same speeches and the same promises right across the country."
About unemployment that is quite true: the same promises right across the country, "no one will suffer". But two years later: not necessarily suffering but suffering if necessary; or let me quote the phrase as it is:
I don't want to see a single day of unnecessary suffering.
I suggest that is not good enough. I say that if they made the same promises right across the country-and I do not deny that they did so-they are breaking them in 1960.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) referred to the fact that it was rather unusual to have a debate on an appropriation bill at this particular time. However, I believe he recognized, as do many of us, that the conditions of today are rather unusual and that we are experiencing a time of boom and bust; that conditions of boom and bust are taking place at one and the same time. For an ever smaller number of Canadians we are indeed experiencing a condition of boom and for an ever growing number of Canadians we are experiencing a period of extremely difficult times indeed.
We have little way of knowing at this particular time whether the bill now before us is adequate to meet the conditions that obtain in the nation because the minister has not yet indicated what the other further supplementary estimates are going to be like. I should like to make a number of observations at this time and at the same time ask the minister a few questions which I hope he will answer either when he participates in this debate at this time or when the house is in committee.

We do not know yet how much the government is intending to spend in the current fiscal year. We have almost reached the end of the current fiscal year. Today is March 7 and there are only 24 days left in the month. Last year the minister presented final supplementary estimates on March 20 in the total of $282,248,993. Therefore when in these supplementary estimates the minister is asking us for $31,960,551 plus loans, investments and advances of $400,000, making a total of $32,360,511, we have a difficult time indeed in knowing what the actions of the government actually are at this time.
I hope the minister will be able to indicate with reasonable accuracy how much more money he anticipates he will be needing after he has received the amount of money for which he is now asking. It is rather hard for us to form an opinion as to the merits of these supplementary estimates until we know the answer to the other supplementary estimates yet to appear. However, we know that over the last number of years the estimates that have been presented to the parliament of Canada have gradually risen. The estimates for the year 1957-58 totalled $4,978,822,907; the estimates for the year ended March 31, 1959 totalled $5,606,870,020; the estimates for the year ending March 31 next, as we now know them, total $5,681,915,047. However, if the last estimates of the fiscal year will equal the last estimates we received on March 20 a year ago, then the whole of the estimates for the current fiscal year would total $5,964,749,757. That would mean that there has been a 6 per cent increase in the estimates for this year as opposed to the estimates of a year ago. When one considers that the population has grown by only 3 per cent, one would hope it would have a much greater effect on the welfare of many more of our people than apparently government expenditures and policies are having.
We do know that the minister is making every effort to make his budget forecasts come true. We also know that if he can accomplish that he has hopes of being able to present a balanced budget to the nation in April or May, or whenever he brings down the budget. However, let us ask ourselves at whose expense are these efforts being made? Who is going to receive the benefits and who is going to pay for the minister being able to accomplish the aims he has set out for himself? We certainly do not agree that any of the prosperity we hear so much about is being shared by the farmers, the veterans, the civil servants, the small businessmen, the small industrialists or the unemployed of Canada.
79951-0-115J
Appropriation Act
Looking at the estimates as a whole we see that agriculture is being voted $10,630,000. I think the minister will agree that the agricultural crisis is harsh enough for those estimates to have absorbed a little higher level of government participation in the welfare of those who till the soil. The Department of Labour has an estimate of $15 million, and he Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) acknowledges that that is only intended to alleviate the plight of a limited number of those who are unemployed. Yet those two matters alone, agriculture and unemployment, I think the government knows full well are not temporary difficulties which we are experiencing, and unless some much more substantial remedies are undertaken the situation in regard both to agriculture and to unemployment is going to continue to be with us and the problem is apt to become worse rather than better.
A number of us in Canada had always expected that if we ever faced more difficult times in our country, then the northern vision would really play a most effective role. Yet in the supplementary estimates I notice that not a nickel is devoted to the northern vision. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) shares in these estimates only to the extent of $2,141,001. Only the $1 has any relationship at all to the northern vision, and we would have expected that at this crucial time in the economic welfare of the Canadian nation as a whole the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources would have found a most open ear on the part of his cabinet colleagues and he would have been pleading with them to make his vision into much more of a reality.
Then we notice a very small estimate for a department which ordinarily is responsible for the employment of much labour in Canada, and I refer to the department of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). Only a small item is contained therein amounting to $450,000.
I have to say these things, Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that we have not yet seen the final supplementary estimates, although I hope that inside of a week or so we will be able to have a look at them. I also hope that those estimates will indicate a much more determined attitude on the part of the government to relieve the hardships and the concern facing so very many Canadians at this time.
I also notice that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) is expecting to receive only $3,500,000. In the light of the debate which took place this afternoon, when the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) so

Appropriation Act
ably indicated the tremendous needs tor airport facilities all over the dominion, this supplementary estimate for the department of the Minister of Transport seems rather insignificant indeed. It does not even seem adequate to meet his assurance to the house that the Dorval airport will be completed this year.
I was particularly interested when I noticed that under loans, investments and advances there is only the sum of $400,000 representing a loan proposed to the government of the Northwest Territories. I had expected that the Minister of Public Works under this head would have had a few hundred million dollars to spend on housing under the authority of the bill he is now attempting to pilot through the House of Commons. However, I notice no such intention as yet.
I hope and I say this for the sake of those who are unemployed in Canada-that the government will desert its present policy as announced the other day apparently of using as little of this housing money as possible until the summer months are over. I hope that the government will move with all haste in this regard, and I certainly expect that in the final supplementary estimates we will see a very large amount for the Minister of Public Works so that we can progressively pursue the continuation of a high level of house building in Canada. Our municipalities would also be able to relieve the plight of many of our unemployed much more adequately if they were able to obtain the capital resources necessary to carry on municipal development, and to meet many of the social needs of our rapidly growing communities in Canada.
I asked the Minister of Labour some days ago whether the government was giving any consideration to reactivating the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, and the minister rather amazed me for the moment when he replied that no municipality had asked for such help from his department. I am sure that even the Minister of Labour must know that the government has often within recent years, especially within the last year, officially been asked by many municipalities, including the association of mayors and reeves, for assistance in order to obtain the necessary capital so that they may proceed with their urban developments.
We know that the problems of the government are great, but at the same time we feel that while the minister last year in his budget speech used the words "recovery which is now well under way", that recovery which is referred to is turning out to be recovery and unprecedented prosperity for

a declining number of Canadian corporations and individuals, and that there is no such thing, indeed, as widespread recovery which would enable the minister to balance his annual financial account. The situation as far as the masses of the people is concerned is indeed deteriorating, and I would plead with the minister to let us have a look at his final estimates as soon as possible. I would hope he can indicate now when he will be in a position to bring down the final supplementary estimates, because much of what I have already said may lose a lot of its validity-and I hope I am shown to be wrong-if and when the minister files the final supplementary estimates.
I am particularly interested to know whether government expenditures are at a level so that those estimates will be equal to last year's or whether they may even exceed last year's. The reason I am raising this subject at this time is because we have seen the intentions of the government clearly revealed in the blue book of estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961, and upon a close analysis of the estimates which have been tabled for the next fiscal year we are very much afraid that the government intends to ride out the storm and not intervene on behalf of the farmers, on behalf of the unemployed, on behalf of the federal civil servants or on behalf of the small businessmen of Canada.
The government seems to be pursuing a policy, as revealed in the estimates now before us and confirmed by the blue book we now have for the next year, of letting nature take its course and allowing the people to be damned, as long as it can boast about the sum total of the figures which are admittedly higher than they were a year ago. We have also had a look at the figures contained in the "Investment Outlook" for this year and, again, these figures underline the suspicion which is abroad in Canada that the government is intending to ride out the storm and let nature take its course. I agree that nature will take its course, but at what expense? Certainly if that is the position of the government it is not in line with its expression of the understanding of the needs of the Canadian people as voiced at election time.
We know that the Minister of Finance is often wrong in his predictions. We know that last year he estimated there would be a 7 per cent increase in the gross national output, adding the qualification that stable prices must be assumed. The minister knows that the population has grown by 3 per cent, while the money supply has been inflated by approximately 2 per cent, so the hon. gentleman is able to boast of only a 2

per cent per capita increase in the volume of goods and services produced last year. Even that small increase is welcomed, because it indicates increased productivity per manhour in Canada.
I should like to ask the minister whether he is able to tell us at this time when he expects to present his annual budget to the House of Commons. I say this because at this time, when we are asked to be happy and satisfied with a $15 million outlay in respect of almost one million unemployed in Canada; when we are asked to be happy with an outlay of only $10 million in respect of the depressed condition of Canadian agriculture; when we see nothing in the supplementary estimates for the hard-pressed municipalities, or for the small industrialists or businessmen, I think it is urgent that we should hear the minister present the budget at as early a date as it is possible for him to do so.
I should like, also, to ask the minister to indicate what is the cash position of the government. On the passing of these estimates are we going to run more heavily into debt and, if so, will that involve the risk of having to issue new currency and thereby increase inflation? The record of the last several years is that the government in respect of loans, investments and advances for the year 1958-59 asked for an increase of $73 million as compared with 1957-58. Then the government apparently decided it had resolved all the problems-I am hoping it was not that it had only managed an election victory. The following year it reduced the expenditure on loans, investments and advances, and I point out that this is one department which is responsible for so much employment in Canada that I cannot ignore it. Before the election, the government raised the amount by $73 million. After the election was over, the figure showed a reduction of $70 million less than the year before and, according to the blue book, the intention of the government for the ensuing year is to spend even less in 1960-61; $64 million less in this department than in the year 1959-60.
We regret these cutbacks in these departments of government which are responsible for supplying employment to the workers of Canada. We agree that balancing the budget is desirable. However, we do not agree that the budget has to be balanced at the expense of the common people of Canada, the farmers, the unemployed, the civil servants and the veterans of our nation, and we feel that this is what is presently taking place. I know there is no election in the offing-or, at least, I think I know- and hence he may think there may be no urgency.

If they are being made to come true by decisions of the government, regardless of the cost to human welfare in Canada, I feel that would be callous treatment indeed to most of our people and I could only put it down to lack of courage to take decisive action or to inability to formulate policy which would resolve the problems facing us in Canada today.

paid to the governments of the provinces, and the provinces have been paying them to the farmers for some considerable time. We all know that. It may be that the provincial treasuries would be faintly incommoded by not getting this money last week instead of this week but, of course, any delay today, as the hon. member for Ottawa West pointed out, does not make the slightest difference, because the Senate does not meet until tomorrow evening. It will be interesting to see whether there will be royal assent tomorrow night or whether we wait until Wednesday. That will be very interesting to see, after all the talk we have heard from the Minister of Finance. Still, nothing that happens today is delaying the payment of this money at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been delayed for the last three weeks.

Of course, whether I am a better judge of the minister's vanity than he is himself, I leave to the committee. The minister knew perfectly well how we were going to vote. He was told that by our leader. We were going to vote for whatever little there is in this bill, notwithstanding the fact that it is most inadequate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Clauses 2 to 4 inclusive agreed to.
On the schedule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the schedule carry?

Oh no, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance said I had introduced nothing new in my statement. Everything in my original statement was new. I did not go over any of the points which had been made previously. I referred to a broadcast made by the Prime Minister after we had ceased to debate the estimates, so I could not have been threshing old straw, unless the minister thinks that the Prime Minister's broadcast was old straw-in fact, most of it, perhaps, was. It was certainly a dim and dizzy vision.
The other thing I referred to was a letter which the Minister of Agriculture did not table until after his item was finished, and I had no opportunity of referring to that letter at an earlier stage because we were denied it. That is precisely what I was complaining about, and that is precisely why I made the speech in the first place. I asked the minister whether or not it was true-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: What clause are you speaking to?

I am speaking to the schedule, as the Minister of Public Works would know if he paid attention to the Chair.

In this schedule there is this item for the fifty-fifty payment to the provinces, and I asked the minister on second reading-and the hon. gentleman could have saved some time if he had answered me then, instead of entering upon all those irrelevancies-if all the treasury board had before it when they put this item in the estimates was the press releases which the Minister of Agriculture said was all he knew about the scheme of the three western provinces.
I think that question deserved an answer. I think it deserves an answer now. Did the government have nothing more from the provinces with regard to how this money was being paid out than the press releases made by these three governments, because that is what the minister told us. I read the extract from Hansard of February 9? I think we are entitled to know. Did the government have the details, or did it have a scheme submitted by those provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What goes on in the treasury board is carried on in confidence, and I have no intention of repeating on the floor of the house the discussions which took place in the treasury board. The members of the treasury board were well acquainted with the background of this matter, this having been well known to the cabinet in the course of these negotiations.
Mr. Chairman, as you will recall, I pointed out in my remarks that the essential point lies in the terms of the item which become part of the appropriation bill. That item is perfectly clear in its terms and in its intent. This is No. 613-
Contributions to the governments of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, of one half the amounts paid by the governments of those provinces to farmers in respect of unharvested crops to a maximum of $300 in respect of any one farm; and to authorize, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, contributions to the governments of those provinces (or their municipalities) in respect of the administrative costs incurred by them in making such payments to farmers.
The terms of that item are perfectly clear, and the enabling provision will be adhered to strictly by the governor in council in accordance with the terms of the bill.
I should like to ask the minister what the terms and the conditions are which are prescribed by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: In other words, what the minister is saying is that this is blank cheque legislation; that this parliament which has to vote the money is not entitled to know how this money is going to be spent. In other words, that once we dispose of this money, and not before, the governor in council will decide under what terms this money is to be spent. Is that what the minister is saying and, if it is not, what is he saying?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not expect the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to know or even to try very hard to understand a situation like this.
Why not answer the question instead of indulging in personal remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Items containing provisions such as this authorizing expenditure in accordance with terms and conditions to be prescribed by the governor in council are quite usual in a supply bill. As a matter of fact, I suppose that during the time the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a minister hundreds of such items were introduced by the government of which he was a member. Suddenly, however, this practice becomes different now that somebody else follows it. It was all right when he and his colleagues were in office. It was perfectly acceptable then; there was nothing wrong with it, but when somebody else does it, it suddenly, out of a clear blue sky, becomes an offence. You know perfectly well, Mr. Chairman, that the offence which rankles in the mind of the hon. member is that he is not sitting on this side of the house.

Oh yes, I am frightfully resentful; very jealous of the minister, I admit. But that really has nothing to do with the business before this committee. The business before this committee is how the public moneys are to be spent, and who is to decide the way in which they are to be spent; whether that decision is to be made by parliament or by the governor in council; whether it is to be made publicly, here in this house, or secretly in the closet afterwards. I have very clear recollections of a great many of these items in the estimates in the period when I was on the other side of the house and for many years before that-long before the hon. member for Eglinton ever came to this parliament-and I cannot remember-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You were the man in the closet.

For the benefit of the Minister of Public Works I might say that the word "closet" and the word "cabinet" are, as
Appropriation Act
he will find out, synonymous. He will find that out by consulting a dictionary. I thought the one word might appeal more to the Minister of Public Works than the other.
I return to the point I was making, namely that I cannot remember a single occasion when Mr. Ilsley or Mr. Abbott-
Who were they?

-or Mr. Harris ever
declined to explain fully the scheme under which moneys-
Scheme?

-would be paid out of the treasury; the scheme-and I used that word in its proper sense-the plan, or the method, by which the moneys were to be paid out. It seems to me that for hon. members who spent a good many years going about this country prating about the rights of parliament to come in here and say, "We will not tell you a thing about how this money is spent and we will not make a decision about how it is to be spent until parliament has acted,"-when parliament would have no further control-is a most extraordinary doctrine. I must say, of course, it is a very typical Tory attitude. It was the attitude taken by the government of Mr. Bennett. It is exactly what the Liberals protested against at that time and I am very glad to take a Liberal attitude at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and some of his colleagues have been trying desperately for the past six or seven weeks to make something out of nothing as far as this particular matter of assistance to the snowed-in crops of farmers in western Canada is concerned. The situation in this regard has been perfectly clear to everybody in the country who has taken any interest at all in the matter from the very beginning.
The dominion government told the provinces that it was willing to ask parliament to pay half the cost of payments of up to $3 an acre for a maximum of 200 acres to farmers whose crops were snowed in to the extent of 50 per cent or more. This was made plain from the very beginning. The provinces were told they could put in any type of scheme they liked and administer it in the way they wished in order to make that payment. The federal government said it would pay 50 per cent of what the provinces paid to the farmers up to $3 an acre in order to provide that assistance. Nothing could be more simple, plain or clear. As soon as parliament met and we had an opportunity to bring in the supplementary estimates we brought in this particular estimate to provide

Appropriation Act
for that payment of 50 per cent of the assistance payments that the provinces made.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has been trying to read into this a disregard for the rights of parliament. He attempts to characterize it as a sinister scheme. In doing so the hon. member is completely off the beam. Of course, he is off the beam with respect to most things but in this case he is more off the beam than usual and every farmer in western Canada will recognize that fact.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to hold up this item but I am just going to say that what the Minister of Agriculture has just said does not happen to be in accordance with the facts as he revealed them himself by making that return several days after the item passed because in that letter from Mr. Hutton, Mr. Hutton asked if the federal government would agree to a particular procedure and the minister waited until we had voted the item and then wrote and said he would agree thinking we would never find it out. This shows that the government did not give the provinces a blank cheque at all, that it insisted on knowing how the provinces were going to spend this money.
What hon. members opposite have refused to do is to tell us. It would have been very simple and all this fuss could have been avoided if the minister had done what he ought to have done in the first place and as anybody with any regard for parliament would have done. If he had got the regulations of the three prairie provinces-the provincial governments that are spending this money-and laid them on the table of the house so we could have read them, all would have been well. Parliament is entitled to know the scheme under which this money was paid out, but the government has consistently denied that to us, to no apparent purpose that I can see because, as the minister says, if we had gone out and asked the provincial governments we could no doubt have found out from them. But parliament has the right to have that information here in this chamber. What astonishes me is that the Prime Minister who talked so much about the rights of parliament could have permitted this course of action. I am not surprised at the Minister of Agriculture but I am surprised at the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance for taking this arrogant attitude that parliament is not entitled to have this information laid on the table for hon. members to examine.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is another straw horse of a most finely ground chaff. There was never any concealment in regard

to any of the documents in connection with this case. I placed the documents on the table as soon as I reached an agreement with the provinces. Everything that was asked for was produced. As a matter of fact, on a simple request from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, without any order being passed in the house, I produced all the correspondence he asked for at any time. What the hon. member was talking about latterly was not this payment at all. He was referring to the administration costs in connection with the payments.
That is quite true, but it is part of the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was not part of the $3 payment.
It is part of the money we are spending.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We had a series of conversations, the provinces and myself, with regard to the method by which the administration costs would be paid. Each province had a different method of carrying on the matter. It was somewhat difficult to arrive at a method which would be equitable to all the provinces as far as the split-up of the administrative costs were concerned. There was never at any time an attempt to conceal anything from parliament. If the hon. member wanted to know what the regulations were at any time all he had to do was to get a copy of them. Thousands of copies were put out by the western provinces outlining what their regulations were.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Pursuant to the order previously made, the bill will now be read a third time.
Is the minister not going to make a speech?

Carried.
Bill read the third time and passed.

Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I assume we will go on with the amendment to go into supply tomorrow? Would the house leader tell us what we will be doing on Wednesday and Thursday and any other day of the week for which the order of business can be announced?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I judge that the opposition tomorrow would want to continue with their amendment to go into supply. The proposed order of business for Wednesday will be, first, the motion in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to

set up a joint committee on Indian affairs. Second, and related to that, we will take the second reading of Bill No. C-2, an act to amend the Indian Act. Third, we will take second reading of Bill No. C-3, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act. Those three motions are all related to Indian affairs.
The fourth order of business will be the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the tenure of office of judges; fifth, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the National Housing Act; and, sixth, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with the Railway Act.
On Thursday, there will be continuation of that business. All this is subject to change, if necessary, although it is unlikely that there would be a change. On Friday, we will continue with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
Business of the House

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask two questions. First, will we be taking the agricultural estimates on Friday in any event? speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In response to the first question, Mr. Speaker, I will announce on Thursday night the order of business for Friday. This is the proposed order of business for the next three days and of course there may be changes. We have considered the other suggestions but I believe the order I have outlined is preferable.
